brief.head: Gates, philosopher
brief.text: Ajay Shah cited “the great philosopher Bill Gates”: the world changes less than you think in one year and more than you think in ten. {081-C02}

brief.head: Danger near home
brief.text: Ajay Shah likened Ding’s late slip to the hiking lesson: the worst accidents happen when you think you have almost reached home and let your guard down. {081-C03}

brief.head: Know your origin
brief.text: Every path leaves its own strengths and blind spots, Ajay Shah said. Know them without whining or beating yourself up, then compensate for weaknesses or bet big on strengths. {081-C08}

brief.head: It takes a village
brief.text: Movements need more than direct doers like Anand and WestBridge, Ajay Shah said. They also need community organisers who keep morale and enthusiasm going. {081-C16}

brief.head: Lost without a guide
brief.text: Ajay Shah worried that Chess960 loses the familiar board casual fans know. Amit Varma replied that without great commentary, fans would be just as lost in classical chess. {081-C11}

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on the chess year of 2024
lead.head: Mate in seven lessons
body: Ajay Shah asked for a tour of chess in 2024. Amit Varma promised more than a tour: in each big chess story of the year, a life lesson that goes beyond chess and into our lives.

It was a great year for Indian chess, Varma said, though it “ended in a slightly ugly manner”. Gukesh Dommaraju won the World Championship, Arjun Erigaisi reached 2809 in the live ratings, and India won gold in both sections of the Olympiad.
Shah, old enough to remember Anand’s journey, marvelled that Gukesh was only eighteen. Yet he felt no tribal rooting. Ding, the champion, was to him “an equally wonderful flawed character”.
Varma shared the feeling. Ding had been world number two in 2019, he said, before Covid and personal troubles; winning the title then broke him mentally.
## A change of position

The match ended on Ding’s 55. Rf2 in Game 14, a move any halfway decent player would avoid in isolation. But the position was not an isolated one, Varma argued. Over a few moves the bishop had drifted to a8 and Gukesh’s king had crept two squares closer. Neither player noticed the change.

The world is not static, Varma said, and we keep missing that. “Mentally all the time we get stuck with one view of the world, and then everything changes, and we don’t realise that it has changed.” {081-C01}

Ding lost the match, in Varma’s reading, off the board as much as on it. His team was small and his fitness poor, and Gukesh, seeing that he looked tired, set out to make every game long. “Being good is not enough. It’s the stuff that goes around it that matters,” Varma said. {081-C04}
## Shaped by the road
Gukesh was trained without computers until he became a grandmaster. Arjun, short of invitations to elite events, had to try to win every game in opens. They grew into very different players.
“It’s not about what you want to do,” Varma said, drawing on a scene from Chaitanya Tamhane’s film *The Disciple*. “It’s who do you want to be.” {081-C07}
Magnus Carlsen, he argued, left the classical world championship because engine preparation had drained the joy out of it. Carlsen chose renewal over mastery, a choice open to all of us.
## Power play
The year’s ugly end belonged to the same Carlsen: his refusal to change out of jeans at the World Rapid in New York, and his proposal to split the World Blitz title with Ian Nepomniachtchi.
Power corrodes character, Varma warned, and much of success is luck. The model for handling it is Vishy Anand, who has power, “but you would never know”. {081-C12}
Even the coverage carried a lesson. Engine bars told viewers that 55. Rf2 was a blunder before most could see it for themselves. Technology, Varma said, should be a tool, not a crutch.
The last word went to Sagar Shah and Amruta Mokal, who built ChessBase India for years out of love, with Sagar shooting on his mobile phone. It now has millions of subscribers.
People overthink new ventures, Varma said. “Act today, have a bias for action, do what you love, things will work out.” {081-C15}

second.label: The Olympiad
second.head: Third board, first prize
second.deck: India’s coach put its top-rated player on board three, and India won gold
body: At the 2024 Olympiad, Arjun Erigaisi was India’s top-rated player. The team coach, Srinath Narayanan, put him on board three, not board one. {081-S06}
His logic, as Amit Varma told it: Arjun is brilliant at beating players rated 2600, and board three is where he would meet them. If the others simply drew, India would still win.

Arjun dominated, and Gukesh, on top board, got something like ten out of eleven. {#tenofeleven} That included a miraculous endgame win over Wei Yi, then China’s top-ranked player, which even Hikaru Nakamura praised. Varma called it perhaps the greatest Olympiad performance of all time, if he was not mistaken. Both the open and the women’s teams took gold.

quote.text: Why board three? Because he’s brilliant at beating twenty six hundreds, and board three is where he’s likely to play them.

second.caption: the board-three gambit

third.head: Look, no computers
body: When Gukesh was a boy, his coach Vishnu Prasanna went to his parents with a proposal, as Amit Varma told it: “Let’s do an experiment. Let’s train him without computers.” {081-S04}

Until he became a grandmaster, Gukesh apparently did not use computers at all. Varma would not say that is the cause, but his calculation is phenomenal: in a complicated middlegame, “there is no one better than him”.
Even Magnus Carlsen, Varma said, has found that Gukesh sees lines in post-game talks that never crossed his mind.

The flip side, critics including Carlsen say, is weird positional intuition. Varma suspects one reason. Around 2020 and 2021, four or five Indians would fill the top five at Titled Tuesday, but never Gukesh. {#titletuesday} His rapid and blitz ratings sit 100 to 150 points below the top.
third.caption: the boy trained without computers

p2.title: Lessons from the board
p2.deck: Chess in 2024, chapter by chapter, and the life lesson Amit Varma drew from each, with Ajay Shah’s additions

sections.label: The first lesson
sections.head: Stuck in the old equilibrium
sections.caption: Ding’s last blunder
body: Game 14 reached an ending in which Gukesh was a pawn up with rooks and bishops still on the board. Amit Varma explained that it was a theoretical draw unless both rooks and both bishops came off.

At move 52 a bishop trade was impossible. By move 54, quietly, the white bishop had gone to a8, with only one diagonal open, and Gukesh’s king had moved two squares closer. Ding, his mind already on the rapid tiebreak, played 55. Rf2.
Gukesh, who said later that he was about to play Rb3, needed a few seconds to see it. Ding realised only from Gukesh’s reaction. Both, Varma said, were stuck in the old equilibrium. {081-S01}
## Strangers in the same house

The lesson, Varma said, is that the world is not static. In work or in love, “the king moves two squares and the bishop goes to A8”, and we do not notice. A specialisation gets taken over by AI; a couple ends up as strangers in the same house. {081-C01}

We cannot update our priors every minute, Varma conceded; it takes too much cognitive energy. But we settle into grooves. Ajay Shah called it status quo bias, and said waking up to change course is one of life’s great skills. {081-C02}
~ Shah, by his own account a very low quality chess player, was surprised to learn that a bishop on a8 can be trapped, with only one diagonal to run along.

quote.text: So both these super strong grandmasters were stuck in the old equilibrium. Neither of them realize what has happened.

sections.label: The second lesson
sections.head: Good is not good enough
sections.caption: the game outside the game
body: The quality of the chess did not decide the match, Amit Varma said. Both players made mistakes; Ding made the last one. What decided it was preparation and attitude, and Ding fell short on both.

His small team meant he was often surprised in the opening and spent an hour or more recovering. He was also not physically fit. As a junior, Varma had learnt that a five-hour game burns as many calories as a boxer loses in a round. {#calories}
Gukesh noticed. “Gukesh said he was looking tired, so we decided I will make him play for as long as possible,” Varma recounted. {081-S02}
## A slight Polish band

Gukesh’s team was built for the job. On Vishy Anand’s suggestion, Grzegorz Gajewski led it; Jan-Krzysztof Duda played more than 300 practice games with him; Radosław Wojtaszek joined too. “Slight Polish band kind of happening here,” Varma said. {081-J04}

Ajay Shah saw a lesson for Indian firms. It would have been easy to stay clubby, “sharing biryani at night” with an all-Indian team. Instead, he said, “They didn’t think in terms of nationality. They just said we’ve got to get a job done.” {081-C05}
~ Shah also saw intergenerational transfer at work: Anand brought knowledge and culture, and each generation hands down something better to the next. {081-C06}

quote.text: Being good is not enough. It’s the stuff that goes around it that matters. It’s the game outside the game.

sections.label: The third lesson
sections.head: Madman by necessity
sections.caption: Gukesh, Arjun and what shapes us
body: Gukesh and Arjun Erigaisi, Amit Varma said, became very different players because of very different journeys.

Players who cross 2700 usually get invited to elite round-robins, where you press with White, accept draws with Black, and six out of ten is a decent score. Arjun did not get those invitations: India already had Pragg, Vidit, Nihal and Harikrishna in the circuit, and no organiser will call four Indians to a ten-player event.
So he played Swiss-system opens against grandmasters rated 2600 to 2650, where every draw cost him rating points. He had to try to win every game. {081-S05}
He grew so wild that Magnus Carlsen called him a madman, and rose from about 2700 to a live peak of 2809, world number two. {#peak-2809}
## What you do, who you become

The lesson: what you do shapes who you are. Varma said his own long-form podcasting, with its demands of patience and listening, may even have changed his character. Scrolling and swiping puts the mind in one rhythm; reading a book or watching good world cinema puts it in another. {081-C07}
~ Varma compared Arjun’s run to Bobby Fischer’s six-nil wins over Taimanov and Larsen, though Fischer’s dominance, over three players including Petrosian, lasted only a limited period.

quote.text: In an open tournament you have to try to win every freaking game.

sections.label: The fourth lesson
sections.head: Mugging up is not chess
sections.caption: why Carlsen left the classical crown
body: Magnus Carlsen did not quit the classical world championship out of petulance, Amit Varma said. He quit because of what engines had done to the game.

Engine evaluations assume perfect play, and humans never play perfectly. So elite preparation has become a hunt for moves that are not optimal but whose refutation only another computer could find. {081-C09}

Before each title match, Carlsen and his team spent six months in camp after camp, because an opponent who knew a computer line he did not could beat him. {#sixmonths} The quality of his life, he concluded in Varma’s telling, had gone to bits. {081-S08}
## Fischer’s old answer

His answer is freestyle, the new name for Fischer Random or Chess960, which Bobby Fischer devised in the 1970s out of the same frustration. The pieces behind the pawns are shuffled identically for both sides, with 960 possible starting positions. {#chess-960}

Carlsen has already lost two Chess960 world titles, to Wesley So and Hikaru Nakamura. He plays anyway. “Mastery is good, renewal is better,” Varma said: a brain surgeon who stops reading new papers is stuck in his groove. {081-C10}
~ Classical chess is alive, Varma insisted: reports of its death are exaggerated. But he expects it to die one day, under a mountain of theory every newcomer must climb.

quote.text: This is not even chess. This is mugging up, mugging up, mugging up. The joy of playing chess isn’t there.
quote.who: Magnus Carlsen, as told by Amit Varma

sections.label: The fifth lesson
sections.head: Who will check the king?
sections.caption: Magnus Carlsen’s misbehaviour
body: Magnus Carlsen, Amit Varma said, is easily the greatest player of all time. Fifteen years of dominance, and a business through Take Take Take, have given him enormous power, and power can affect people in negative ways.

In 2022 Carlsen lost to Hans Niemann at the Sinquefield Cup, withdrew and called him a cheat. Varma gave him the benefit of the doubt at first, then stopped within months. Nobody offered a plausible way to cheat over the board, and Carlsen never apologised. “Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence,” Varma said. {081-S09}

Then came Jeansgate, and at the World Blitz a proposal to split the title with Ian Nepomniachtchi. Video later caught Carlsen suggesting that, if FIDE refused, they play one short draw after another. “It’s basically a kind of match fixing,” Varma said. {081-S11}
## Judge the act
Borrowing a line from Niemann, Varma asked listeners to judge the act, not the name: “forget it is Magnus Carlsen, forget it’s the greatest player of all time”. {081-C13}

Power corrodes character, he said, and much of success is luck. Carlsen risks becoming Vladimir Kramnik, a great champion turned embittered accuser. The model is Vishy Anand: powerful, soft-spoken, working behind the scenes. {081-C12}
~ Varma hoped that Carlsen, who seemed super stressed out through the last day of blitz, comes out of this phase.

quote.text: Do you think Vishy Anand doesn’t have power? Oh man, he has power. But you would never know.

sections.label: The sixth lesson
sections.head: Engine on, brain off
sections.caption: computers and coverage
body: Amit Varma watched 55. Rf2 on Sagar Shah’s stream. The moment it was played, the computer evaluation changed on screen and everybody stood up. Only Tania Sachdev, he thought, worked it out from the board; even Sagar glanced at the computer to make sure.
On David Howell’s broadcast there was no engine evaluation. Howell took about as long as Gukesh to see the blunder, Varma said, because he was thinking on his own. {081-S14}
## A tool, not a crutch

The lesson reaches beyond chess. Use ChatGPT for ideas and to polish your prose, Varma said, but do the writing yourself so your brain keeps working. “If you use it as a crutch, you dumb yourself down.” {081-C14}
Ajay Shah’s gloss was shorter: “you stop experiencing life”. Varma agreed, because you stop thinking about the chess.
Varma also bristled at audiences who clap when a player finds the engine’s top move. “Are you guys morons? There are probably four or five moves which are fine here.” {081-J07}
~ His advice to viewers: watch coverage in which strong grandmasters talk about the position, with the evaluation bar switched off.

quote.text: Howell took as much time to figure out it’s a blunder as Gukesh did. You can actually time them.

side.boxTitle: The boy who said he would
side.boxText: Gukesh, the champion at eighteen, was trained without computers until he became a grandmaster. At eleven he told Sagar Shah he wanted to be the youngest world champion. “And here we are,” Amit Varma said. {#youngest}

contQuote.text: And Sagar and Amruta showed us a way by diving into something for the love of it. And that’s my lesson to everyone. If you’re watching this, that’s all you need.

p3.title: Stories of the year
p3.deck: Jeans, a guru’s silence, a president’s reply and a channel built on love

stories.start: Magnus started really badly. This is critical to note.
stories.end: But Magnus does does this and it is deplorable.
stories.caption: Jeansgate
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on Magnus Carlsen, a dress code and FIDE
stories.head: A principle nobody could name
body: The World Rapid Championship in New York, held on Wall Street and planned by FIDE for months, was magnificently organised, Amit Varma said. Magnus Carlsen started badly, with two and a half points out of five on day one. {#twoandhalf}

On day two he showed up in jeans, otherwise perfectly turned out in blazer and boots. Every player signs up to the dress code, and jeans break it. Ian Nepomniachtchi, that day or the day before, had been told to change out of sneakers, and did.

The players’ rooms were three minutes away. Carlsen was told he need not change at once, only before round nine. He refused, and later said on Take Take Take that he had decided on principle not to change. {081-S10}

Varma wondered “what is this principle that on principle you refuse to follow a rule”. FIDE, bound to treat everyone equally, would not pair him. Carlsen withdrew from the Rapid and the Blitz, and on Take Take Take said “Fuck you” to FIDE “in exactly these many words”. {081-J08}

Varma thinks the rule itself stupid; Jimmy Carter, he noted, made jeans acceptable as president. But the rule was there and everyone had agreed to it. Had Carlsen been winning, Varma doubted there would have been a tantrum.

Then Carlsen went over the heads of the chief executive, Emil Sutovsky, and the vice-president, Vishy Anand, to the president, Arkady Dvorkovich, who let him back into the Blitz in jeans. There were, Carlsen said, “no grown-ups in FIDE”, and Anand was not up for the job.
~ Varma called it outrageous behaviour. Sutovsky and Anand, he said, are complete gentlemen.
stories.why: FIDE’s hands were tied, Amit Varma argued: it has to treat everyone equally. But a bad mood met star power, and a plain dress code became an ego thing, settled only when the president gave way.

stories.start: It's a great film called The Disciple by Chatanya Tamane.
stories.end: Moment of silence, and then he adds, But don't come for class anymore.
stories.caption: a guru, a band and a choice
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s film recommendation, and a guru’s condition
stories.head: Join the band, leave the class
body: In Chaitanya Tamhane’s film *The Disciple*, Sharad Nerulkar is a purist singer of Hindustani classical music who teaches a class. One day a student’s mother waits patiently to speak to him.

Her son wants to join a college fusion band, she says. One member will sing Western rock in English; her son will sing the classical music he has been taught. He will not join without his guru’s permission, and his mother clearly wants him to.
Nerulkar tells the boy that yes, he can join them. A moment of silence follows. Then he adds: “But don’t come for class anymore.” {081-S07}
~ Bizarre as it may seem, Amit Varma said, the point is that what you do shapes what you are. The boy was nowhere near ready, and the choice was his: who did he want to be? {081-C07}
stories.why: Doing something again and again changes the kind of person you become. Amit Varma’s test for the scroll or the book is the same as the guru’s: not what you want to do, but who you want to be.

stories.start: The first was a conference of Vaklak Havel when he was a head
stories.end: In that case I will make sure I tell him that he's wrong.
stories.caption: Havel and Lee Kuan Yew
stories.kicker: Two stories from Salil Tripathi, retold by Amit Varma
stories.head: First, let the hungry speak
body: The journalist Salil Tripathi, Amit Varma’s guest on a coming episode of *The Seen and the Unseen*, once put a question to Václav Havel, then head of state of Czechoslovakia, at a press conference.

Some argue, Salil said, that free speech is not the most important right, and that you have to feed people first. Havel disagreed: “Because without free speech, how will a hungry man even be able to communicate that he’s hungry?” {081-S12}

Then Havel asked who argued otherwise. The person you are meeting this afternoon, Salil replied: Lee Kuan Yew. Silence fell over the hall. Then Havel said that in that case, he would make sure he told him he was wrong.
~ Varma loved the anecdote for what it tells you about what a principled man Havel was.
stories.why: Havel held his line when it was diplomatically awkward. Power corrupts, as the saying goes, and absolute power corrupts absolutely; not only in governments, Varma said: power and success can corrode anyone’s character. {081-J17}
stories.postscript: Nelson Mandela, asked by Salil to speak up for Aung San Suu Kyi, declined: “that was prisoner Mandela. This is President Mandela.” {081-S13}

stories.start: So one of the most beautiful little clips that I saw after Gukesh one
stories.end: showed us a way by diving into something for the love of it
stories.caption: Sagar Shah and Amruta Mokal
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on the couple behind ChessBase India
stories.head: A mobile phone and a long game
body: The morning after Gukesh won, Sagar Shah and Amruta Mokal flew to Singapore. Gukesh hugged Sagar, then saw Amruta, and went and hugged her too. These two, Amit Varma said, are so important to Indian chess.

Sagar, an International Master who never made grandmaster, ran ChessBase India with Amruta for years as a labour of love. “Often he would just go and he would shoot with his mobile phone, using the sound of the mobile phone,” Varma said. {081-S15}

He went to under-11 and district events and talked to small kids and women players. For three, four, five years, Varma thinks, the views went nowhere. {#views} During Covid, with help from the comedian Samay Raina, the channel exploded; it now has millions of subscribers.
~ One old clip shows an eleven-year-old Gukesh telling Sagar he wants to be the youngest world champion.
stories.why: Varma would give the second Bharat Ratna for chess, after Vishy Anand, to these two. People overthink new ventures, he said; Sagar and Amruta simply kept showing up, for years, out of love. {081-C15}

quiz.q: Which move in Game 14 handed Gukesh the world title?
quiz.a: 55. Rf2, allowing a rook trade and then a forced bishop trade.

quiz.q: Why did Srinath Narayanan put India’s top-rated player, Arjun Erigaisi, on board three at the Olympiad?
quiz.a: Arjun is brilliant at beating 2600-rated players, and board three is where he’d face them.

quiz.q: What experiment did Vishnu Prasanna propose to the young Gukesh’s parents?
quiz.a: To train him without computers, which he apparently did until he became a grandmaster.

quiz.q: According to a factoid Amit Varma learnt as a junior, what does a five-hour game burn?
quiz.a: As many calories as a boxer loses in a round of boxing.

quiz.q: Why did Ajay Shah think Gukesh’s team held a lesson for Indian firms?
quiz.a: It was built for the job, not nationality: almost entirely a multinational team.

quiz.q: What did Nelson Mandela tell Salil Tripathi when asked to speak up for Aung San Suu Kyi?
quiz.a: That was prisoner Mandela; this was President Mandela, imprisoned by the presidency.
